title: Two months of abdominal discomfort and an erratic bowel habit in a 26-year-old IT analyst
desc: This station involves a focused history and examination of a 26-year-old IT analyst in general practice with 2 months of vague, intermittent lower abdominal discomfort, bloating and alternating diarrhoea and constipation. She had food poisoning 6 months ago, her job is stressful, she drinks milk-based bubble tea, and she is worried about bowel cancer. The candidate then reads her bloods, coeliac serology, faecal calprotectin and stool tests, all normal, makes a working diagnosis of irritable bowel syndrome (mixed type, possibly post-infectious), explains it positively and plans first-line management with clear safety netting.
focus: Chronic lower GI symptoms in a young adult: screening for red flags, ruling out organic disease with first-line tests, and making and explaining a positive diagnosis of IBS
stem: You are a final-year medical student on placement in a general practice. Jessica, a 26-year-old IT analyst, has come in because she has had discomfort in her abdomen for 2 months. Your supervising GP has asked you to see her first.
tasks: Take a focused history from Jessica and perform a focused examination, telling the examiner what you are examining (10 minutes).

The examiner will give you Jessica's blood tests, coeliac serology, faecal calprotectin and stool test results. Interpret them, then outline your management approach and your safety netting (5 minutes).
patient:
Role: You are Jessica, a 26-year-old IT analyst. You are tired of feeling unwell, a bit embarrassed talking about your bowels, and quietly scared it is something serious. The examiner gives examination findings from the Exam findings below when the candidate says what they are examining.

Opening line: "I've had this discomfort in my tummy for about two months and it just won't go away." (wave vaguely over your lower abdomen)

The pain (give only when asked):

  • Site: you gesture vaguely. If pressed: "Sort of down here on the left, around my belly button, and down on the right. I can't pinpoint it."
  • Started slowly about 2 months ago.
  • Comes and goes. Some days are better than others.
  • Usually a dull, crampy discomfort, about 4 out of 10. Sometimes it goes sharp just before you need to open your bowels: "I have to go and find a toilet ASAP." It eases a bit once you have been.
  • It doesn't really go anywhere else.
  • If asked how bad it is overall: "It's really bad. It's taking over my life." You have taken several days off work because of it.
  • If asked what makes it worse: "Like what?" If the candidate prompts: stress makes it worse, especially at the end of the month when you prepare reports; and it is worse when you have had a lot of dairy (lactose).

Other bowel symptoms (only if asked):

  • Lots of bloating and your tummy swells up; lots of wind.
  • Bowels: 3 to 4 days of loose diarrhoea, 2 to 3 times a day, then a spell of constipation with small hard "pebbles", then diarrhoea again. Constipation is less frequent than the diarrhoea.
  • Urgency when the diarrhoea comes.
  • Sometimes you feel a bit nauseated.

Say no to all of these if asked:

  • Blood in your poo, black tarry poo, or vomiting blood.
  • Vomiting.
  • Yellow skin or eyes, itch.
  • Weight loss: your weight has been steady.
  • Waking at night to open your bowels or with pain.
  • Fevers, night sweats.
  • Mouth ulcers, sore joints, red or painful eyes, skin rashes.
  • Burning or stinging when passing urine, going more often, blood in the urine.
  • Cough, cold or flu symptoms, or anyone around you being sick.
  • Recent travel, camping or drinking untreated water, or eating undercooked food.

Diet (only if asked): you cook for yourself and often eat out with colleagues. You eat bread, pasta and noodles normally; you have not cut out gluten. You drink milk-based bubble tea most days with colleagues, even though you think dairy might upset you.

Periods (only if asked): regular, last period 2 weeks ago. The tummy symptoms are not linked to your cycle. No painful periods, no pain with sex. No chance you are pregnant: you are not in a relationship at the moment.

Past medical history: about 6 months ago you were admitted to hospital overnight with gastroenteritis after food poisoning from a restaurant meal; you had a drip. Your bowels never fully settled after that, and for the last 2 months they have got much worse. No operations. Nothing else.

Medications: melatonin at night (you have trouble sleeping) and vitamin D (a blood test last year showed a low level). No other medicines, no anti-inflammatories, no recent antibiotics.

Allergies:

  • Bee sting: anaphylaxis.
  • "Maybe lactose?" Never tested or diagnosed. You still drink bubble tea.

Family history:

  • Mum: had H. pylori and has reflux (GORD).
  • Dad: type 2 diabetes.
  • Your siblings are well: "I'm the unlucky one."
  • No one in the family has had bowel cancer, Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis or coeliac disease.

Social history:

  • Live alone. You moved to a new city for a new job as an IT analyst: well paid but stressful, and you don't know many people yet.
  • No exercise. Evenings are mostly Netflix binges.
  • Non-smoker. Alcohol: 2 to 3 drinks occasionally. No drugs.
  • Mood (only if asked): stressed and a bit lonely, sleep is poor, but you are not low most of the time and have no thoughts of self-harm.

Ideas, concerns, expectations:

  • Ideas: "I don't know. Maybe something I'm eating?"
  • Concern: bowel cancer.
  • Expectation: you want to find out what is wrong and get back to work properly.

Question to raise once in Part 1: "Do I have bowel cancer?"

Exam findings (examiner gives when the candidate says what they examine)

  • General: well, comfortable, not pale or jaundiced. Weight 58 kg, height 165 cm, BMI 21.
  • Observations: temperature 36.7 °C, HR 76 regular, BP 116/72, RR 14, SpO2 99% on room air.
  • Hands: no clubbing, koilonychia or palmar pallor.
  • Eyes and mouth: conjunctivae pink, no scleral icterus, no episcleritis. No mouth ulcers or angular stomatitis.
  • Neck: no cervical or supraclavicular lymph nodes.
  • Skin and joints: no rash (no erythema nodosum, no itchy blistering rash on elbows or knees). Joints normal.
  • Abdomen, inspection: mildly distended, no scars.
  • Abdomen, palpation: soft. Mild tenderness across the lower abdomen (left and right iliac fossae), no guarding or rebound. No masses, including in the right iliac fossa. No hepatosplenomegaly.
  • Percussion and auscultation: tympanic, no shifting dullness. Bowel sounds normal.
  • Perianal inspection and rectal examination (if offered, with a chaperone): no skin tags, fissures or fistulae; soft brown stool on the glove, no blood or mass.
  • Chest and heart (if examined): normal.

check.x: Professionalism
Performs hand hygiene, introduces self, confirms Jessica's identity and gains consent.
Uses plain language, acknowledges the impact on her work and life, and responds to her worry about bowel cancer with empathy, neither dismissing it nor giving false reassurance before the assessment.
History
Characterises the pain:

kids.x: Site and radiation: vague lower abdomen (left iliac fossa, umbilical, right iliac fossa), cannot pinpoint, no radiation.
Onset and pattern: gradual over 2 months, intermittent with better days; dull and crampy, about 4/10.
Relation to defecation: sharp before a bowel motion with urgency, eases a bit afterwards.
Aggravating factors: stress (month-end reports) and large amounts of dairy.
kids.d: Award if the candidate prompts with examples after she asks "Like what?".

check.x: Characterises the bowel habit and associated symptoms: loose stools 2 to 3 times a day for 3 to 4 days alternating with hard pebble-like stools, urgency, marked bloating and distension, flatulence and occasional nausea.
Screens for red flags:

kids.x: Weight loss, nocturnal symptoms, and fevers or night sweats (none).

check.x: Asks about infective causes: travel, untreated water, undercooked food, sick contacts and fever (none), and elicits the hospital admission with food-poisoning gastroenteritis 6 months ago.
Takes a dietary history: eats gluten (bread, pasta, noodles) normally, drinks milk-based bubble tea most days, and eats out often.
check.d: Award if the candidate establishes current gluten intake (relevant to coeliac serology) and dairy intake.

check.x: Asks about extraintestinal features of IBD or coeliac disease: mouth ulcers, joint pain, red eyes, skin rash (none).
Asks about urinary symptoms and takes a menstrual history: no urinary symptoms; regular periods, no link to her cycle, no dysmenorrhoea or dyspareunia, not pregnant.
Takes the medication and allergy history: melatonin and vitamin D, no NSAIDs or recent antibiotics; bee sting anaphylaxis and a possible, undiagnosed lactose intolerance.
Takes a family history, specifically asking about bowel cancer, inflammatory bowel disease and coeliac disease (none); mother H. pylori and GORD, father type 2 diabetes, siblings well.
Takes a social history: lives alone after moving for a new, stressful job, days off work, no exercise, non-smoker, occasional alcohol (2 to 3 drinks); screens mood and sleep.
Explores her ideas, concerns and expectations: wonders about food, worried about bowel cancer, wants an answer and to get back to work.
Examination
Asks for vital signs, weight and BMI, and notes they are normal (afebrile, BMI 21).
Looks for signs of anaemia, malabsorption and systemic disease: pallor, clubbing, koilonychia, jaundice, mouth ulcers, lymph nodes, eye, skin and joint signs.

Examines the abdomen: inspects (mild distension), palpates all regions for tenderness (mild lower abdominal, no guarding) and masses including the right iliac fossa, liver and spleen, and listens for bowel sounds.
Offers a perianal inspection and rectal examination with a chaperone, looking for skin tags, fissures, fistulae, blood or a mass.
Summarises the examination: well, no alarm signs, mild distension and mild diffuse lower abdominal tenderness only.
Interpretation
Interprets the bloods: normal haemoglobin, MCV, ferritin, B12 and folate (no anaemia, iron deficiency or malabsorption), normal CRP (no systemic inflammation), and normal UEC, LFTs and TSH.
Interprets the coeliac serology: tTG-IgA negative with a normal total IgA, so the test is valid; because she is eating gluten, coeliac disease is very unlikely.
Interprets the faecal calprotectin: 28 µg/g, below 50, so significant bowel inflammation and inflammatory bowel disease are unlikely.
Interprets the stool microscopy, culture and PCR: no pathogens, including Giardia, and no red or white cells.

Gives irritable bowel syndrome, mixed type (possibly post-infectious), as the most likely diagnosis and justifies it: pain linked to defecation, change in stool frequency and form, bloating, stress and food triggers, no red flags, and normal first-line tests.
Notes that 2 months does not meet the Rome IV duration criteria and calls it a working diagnosis to confirm at review.
Gives differentials, each with a feature for or against:
check.d: Credit other reasonable differentials (e.g. endometriosis, small intestinal bacterial overgrowth) given with a feature for or against.

kids.x: Inflammatory bowel disease: diarrhoea, urgency and lower abdominal pain; against: no blood, weight loss or nocturnal symptoms, normal CRP and calprotectin.
Coeliac disease: bloating and diarrhoea; against: negative tTG-IgA with normal IgA while eating gluten, normal ferritin and folate.
Colorectal cancer: change in bowel habit; against: age 26, no bleeding, weight loss, anaemia or family history, normal examination and calprotectin.

Persisting infection such as giardiasis, or lactose intolerance: gastroenteritis 6 months ago and dairy as a trigger; against: negative stool PCR, and lactose does not explain the alternating constipation.
kids.d: Award for either with a feature for or against.

check.x: Management

Explains IBS positively in plain words: a real and common condition of a sensitive, over-reactive gut (gut-brain interaction), which does not damage the bowel or lead to cancer, and answers whether it is "all in her head": the symptoms are real, not imagined, though stress can make them worse.

Gives dietary advice, at least two of: regular meals and fewer triggers (caffeine, alcohol, fatty and gas-producing food); a 2 to 4 week lactose trial (lactose-free or plant milk in her bubble tea); a dietitian-led low FODMAP diet if symptoms persist.

Offers symptom-directed medicines: an antispasmodic (for example mebeverine 135 mg three times daily before meals) or peppermint oil for cramping, loperamide when needed for diarrhoea days, soluble fibre (psyllium) or macrogol for constipation, and low-dose amitriptyline later if pain persists.
check.d: Award for at least two symptom-matched options.

check.x: Addresses stress and lifestyle: regular exercise, sleep and stress management, and psychological therapy (CBT or gut-directed hypnotherapy, with a mental health treatment plan if needed).
Safety netting

Answers her worry about bowel cancer honestly: with no warning signs and normal tests, cancer is very unlikely, so a colonoscopy is not needed now, but it would be if bleeding, weight loss or anaemia developed.

Tells her to see the GP promptly for blood in or black poo, weight loss, waking at night with pain or diarrhoea, fevers, or persistent vomiting, and to go to the ED for severe constant pain, heavy bleeding or feeling faint.
check.d: Award for at least three red flags in plain words linked to where to go.

check.x: Arranges follow-up: GP review in about 4 to 6 weeks with a food and symptom diary to assess the lactose trial and treatment, confirm the diagnosis once symptoms have lasted long enough, and refer to a dietitian if not improving, or gastroenterology referral for new red flags or no response; offers reliable written information.

part2.lead: Jessica had blood and stool tests after your first consultation and has come back a week later for the results. Here they are.
part2.patient:
Ask these questions once each while the candidate explains the plan:

  • "If all my tests are normal, does that mean it's all in my head?"
  • "Do I have to give up bubble tea?"

You are relieved that the tests are normal and that it is not cancer, but you want to know what you can actually do about it. If the candidate uses jargon such as "IBS", "FODMAP" or "calprotectin" without explaining it, ask what it means.

handover.label: Blood tests
handover.model:
• Read: haemoglobin 134, MCV 88, white cells and platelets normal. CRP 2. Ferritin 48, B12 and folate normal. Electrolytes, creatinine, liver tests and albumin normal. TSH normal.
  • For Jessica: no anaemia or iron deficiency (against bleeding, cancer, coeliac disease and IBD), no low B12 or folate (against malabsorption), a normal CRP (no systemic inflammation), and a normal TSH (thyroid disease is not driving the bowel habit).
  • What it changes: no alarm features in the bloods, which supports a positive diagnosis of IBS without colonoscopy now. A normal CRP alone does not exclude IBD; the calprotectin adds to it.

labs.title: Electrolytes, urea, creatinine and liver function

handover.label: Coeliac serology
handover.result: Laboratory comment: serology is reliable only while the patient is eating gluten. Endomysial antibody not performed because tTG-IgA is negative with a normal total IgA.
handover.model:
• Read: total IgA normal, so the IgA-based test is valid; tTG-IgA and DGP-IgG negative.
  • For Jessica: she eats bread, pasta and noodles normally, so a negative tTG-IgA with normal IgA makes coeliac disease very unlikely.
  • What it changes: no duodenal biopsy is needed. She should not start a gluten-free diet on this basis. Had she been IgA deficient, an IgG-based test (DGP-IgG or tTG-IgG) would be needed; had she cut out gluten, the test would need repeating after a gluten challenge.

handover.label: Faecal calprotectin
handover.result: Single stool sample, collected 5 days ago. Laboratory comment: a result below 50 µg/g makes inflammatory bowel disease unlikely.
handover.model:
• Read: 28 µg/g, below the 50 µg/g cut-off.
  • For Jessica: no evidence of significant intestinal inflammation, so IBD is unlikely; with no red flags this supports IBS.
  • What it changes: with the absence of red flags, it helps decide who needs referral for colonoscopy. A normal result means no colonoscopy now. A raised or borderline result would have prompted a repeat test or gastroenterology referral. It does not exclude cancer by itself, which is why red flags still matter.

handover.label: Stool microscopy, culture and PCR
handover.result: Faeces, single specimen, collected 5 days ago. Macroscopic: brown, semi-formed, no visible blood or mucus.
handover.model:
• Read: no red or white cells on microscopy, no ova, cysts or parasites, no bacterial pathogens grown, and a negative multiplex PCR including Giardia, Cryptosporidium and Entamoeba histolytica.
  • For Jessica: no persisting infection 6 months after her food poisoning, and no giardiasis to explain the bloating, wind and loose stools. The absence of white cells is also against inflammatory colitis.
  • What it changes: no antimicrobial treatment is needed. Her gastroenteritis 6 months ago raises the possibility that this is post-infectious IBS.

ask: You are now handing Jessica over to your supervising GP. Please give an ISBAR handover of Jessica, including your interpretation of these results.
What is your most likely diagnosis, and what else would you consider? Justify your answer.
Outline your management of Jessica now, here in general practice.
Before Jessica leaves today, what would you tell her and what follow-up would you arrange?
expect:
• Identify: self, medical student; Jessica, 26, IT analyst.
  • Situation: back for results of tests for 2 months of lower abdominal discomfort and altered bowel habit; all normal.
  • Background: vague cramping pain before bowel motions with urgency, alternating diarrhoea and hard stools, bloating and wind; worse with stress and dairy. No bleeding, weight loss or night symptoms. Food-poisoning admission 6 months ago. No family history of bowel cancer, IBD or coeliac disease. Bee sting anaphylaxis. Examination: mild distension and lower tenderness only.
  • Assessment: normal FBC, ferritin, B12, folate, CRP, UEC, LFTs, TSH; coeliac serology negative with normal IgA while eating gluten; calprotectin 28; stool tests negative. Probable IBS, mixed type.
  • Recommendation: explain diagnosis, diet and lactose trial, symptom-directed treatment, review in 4 to 6 weeks; no colonoscopy now.

Most likely: irritable bowel syndrome, mixed type, possibly post-infectious. Pain related to defecation, change in frequency and form, bloating, stress and dairy triggers, no red flags, normal tests. Only 2 months of symptoms, so a working diagnosis to confirm at review.

  • IBD: diarrhoea, urgency; against: no blood or weight loss, normal CRP and calprotectin.
  • Coeliac disease: bloating, diarrhoea; against: negative tTG-IgA, normal IgA, eating gluten.
  • Colorectal cancer: changed bowel habit; against: 26, no bleeding, anaemia, weight loss or family history.
  • Giardiasis or persisting infection: recent gastroenteritis; against: negative stool PCR.
  • Lactose intolerance: dairy trigger; against: does not explain the constipation.

1. Explain IBS positively: a real, common disorder of gut-brain interaction; does not damage the bowel or cause cancer. Answers "is it in my head?": no, the symptoms are real; stress can make them worse.
  2. Diet: regular meals, less caffeine, alcohol and fatty food; 2 to 4 week trial of reducing lactose with a symptom diary. Bubble tea: try lactose-free or plant milk for a few weeks rather than giving it up. Dietitian-led low FODMAP diet if it persists.
  3. Medicines by symptom: antispasmodic (mebeverine 135 mg three times daily before meals) or peppermint oil for cramps; loperamide when needed for diarrhoea; psyllium or macrogol for constipation; low-dose amitriptyline later for persistent pain.
  4. Stress and lifestyle: exercise, sleep, stress management; CBT or gut-directed hypnotherapy (mental health treatment plan if needed).

• Bowel cancer worry: with no warning signs and normal tests, cancer is very unlikely; no colonoscopy now, but it would be needed if bleeding, weight loss or anaemia developed.
  • See the GP promptly for blood in or black poo, weight loss, waking at night with pain or diarrhoea, fevers, or vomiting that won't settle.
  • Go to the ED for severe constant pain, heavy bleeding, or feeling faint.
  • Follow-up: GP review in 4 to 6 weeks with a food and symptom diary to judge the lactose trial and treatment and confirm the diagnosis; dietitian referral if not improving; gastroenterology referral for new red flags, abnormal results or no response. Offer reliable written information.

ddx.dx: Irritable bowel syndrome, mixed type (possibly post-infectious)
ddx.for: Lower abdominal pain before bowel motions with urgency, alternating loose and hard stools, bloating, triggers of stress and dairy, gastroenteritis 6 months ago, and normal bloods, coeliac serology, calprotectin and stool tests.
ddx.against: Only 2 months of symptoms, so the Rome IV duration criteria are not yet met.

ddx.dx: Inflammatory bowel disease (Crohn's disease or ulcerative colitis)
ddx.for: Loose stools with urgency and lower abdominal pain in a young adult, with days off work.
ddx.against: No blood, weight loss, night symptoms or extraintestinal features, no right iliac fossa mass, and a normal CRP and calprotectin of 28.
Negative tTG-IgA with a normal total IgA while eating gluten, and normal ferritin and folate.

ddx.for: A change in bowel habit over 2 months.
ddx.against: Aged 26 with no rectal bleeding, weight loss, anaemia or family history, a normal examination and a normal calprotectin.

ddx.dx: Persisting enteric infection such as giardiasis
ddx.for: Food-poisoning gastroenteritis 6 months ago, with bloating, wind and loose stools.
ddx.against: No travel or untreated water, and a negative stool microscopy, culture and PCR including Giardia.

ddx.for: Symptoms worse with large amounts of dairy, and she drinks milk-based bubble tea most days.
ddx.against: Does not explain the episodes of hard, pebble-like stools or the link with stress.

guide:
This is a general practice station, so there is no observation chart: give the observations from the Exam findings when the candidate asks for them. In Part 1, give findings only when the candidate says what they are examining. If the candidate asks for tests in Part 1, say the results will be given in Part 2. Jessica asks "Do I have bowel cancer?" once in Part 1; accept a holding answer that the tests will help, with empathy. In Part 2 hand over all four results, then ask the four questions in order. Jessica asks her two questions once each during the management answer.

Accept "irritable bowel syndrome" as the diagnosis. Item 28 is a separate mark for a candidate who notes that 2 months of symptoms does not yet meet the Rome IV duration criteria and calls it a working diagnosis to confirm at review. Accept any reasonable symptom-directed medicines; doses are not required for the mark.

A high-performing candidate characterises the pain and its link to bowel motions, describes the alternating bowel habit, screens systematically for red flags (bleeding, weight loss, night symptoms, family history), and covers gluten and dairy intake, the previous gastroenteritis and her stress. In Part 2 they read the normal results with purpose (valid coeliac serology because IgA is normal and she eats gluten; calprotectin below 50 makes IBD unlikely), make a positive diagnosis of IBS rather than "nothing wrong", explain it without implying it is psychological, answer the cancer worry honestly, and give a practical plan with a lactose trial, symptom-directed treatment, stress management, clear red flags and review.

A borderline candidate takes a generic history without red flags or a family history, calls normal results "nothing wrong", tells her it is stress or "in her head", orders a colonoscopy without indication, or gives no plan for follow-up.
explain:
Diagnosis

Jessica most likely has irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), mixed type, possibly post-infectious after the food-poisoning gastroenteritis 6 months ago. She has recurrent lower abdominal pain related to defecation, with a change in both stool frequency and form (loose stools 2 to 3 times a day alternating with hard pebbles), bloating, distension and wind. Her symptoms are worse with stress and with large amounts of dairy. She has no red flags, her examination shows only mild distension and lower abdominal tenderness, and her first-line tests are normal.

IBS is often thought of as a diagnosis of exclusion, and vague symptoms bring many differentials, so serious causes are excluded first. But once red flags are absent and a small set of first-line tests is normal, IBS should be made as a positive diagnosis rather than leaving the patient with "nothing wrong", and repeated or invasive tests are avoided.

Rome IV criteria

IBS: recurrent abdominal pain on average at least 1 day a week in the last 3 months, associated with at least two of: related to defecation; a change in stool frequency; a change in stool form. The criteria must be met for the last 3 months, with symptom onset at least 6 months before diagnosis. Subtypes depend on stool form on abnormal days (Bristol stool chart): IBS-D, IBS-C, IBS-M (both hard and loose stools more than a quarter of the time) or unclassified. Jessica's symptoms have lasted only 2 months, so strictly this is a working diagnosis that is confirmed at review. Post-infectious IBS follows an episode of infectious gastroenteritis; her bowels never fully settled after it and have worsened over the last 2 months, so it is a possible contributor.

Red flags

Rectal bleeding, melaena, unintentional weight loss, nocturnal symptoms, iron deficiency anaemia, fever, a palpable mass, a family history of colorectal cancer, IBD or coeliac disease, and new symptoms at an older age. Even in a young patient, colorectal cancer stays on the list: young-onset colorectal cancer is rising, and rectal bleeding with a change in bowel habit warrants colonoscopy at any age. Jessica has none of these.

Differentials that matter

  • Inflammatory bowel disease (ulcerative colitis or Crohn's disease): diarrhoea, urgency and pain fit, but there is no blood, weight loss, night symptoms or extraintestinal feature, and the CRP and calprotectin are normal.
  • Coeliac disease: can mimic IBS with bloating and diarrhoea; negative tTG-IgA with a normal total IgA on a gluten-containing diet makes it very unlikely.
  • Colorectal cancer: must be considered with any change in bowel habit; very unlikely without red flags at 26.
  • Bowel infection such as giardiasis: bloating, wind and loose stools after gastroenteritis; stool PCR is negative.
  • Lactose intolerance: may be contributing (dairy trigger) and is worth a trial of reduction, but does not explain the constipation.
  • In a woman, endometriosis can cause bowel symptoms; it is less likely because her symptoms are not cyclical and she has no dysmenorrhoea or dyspareunia.

Interpreting the results

  • Bloods: no anaemia, iron, B12 or folate deficiency, and a normal CRP: no evidence of bleeding, malabsorption or systemic inflammation. Normal TSH, UEC and LFTs.
  • Coeliac serology: tTG-IgA is the first-line test, always with a total IgA, because IgA deficiency (more common in coeliac disease) causes false negatives; in IgA deficiency, IgG-based tests (DGP-IgG or tTG-IgG) are used instead. Endomysial antibody and DGP are supporting tests. Serology is valid only while the patient is eating gluten; if gluten has been cut out, a gluten challenge is needed before testing. Diagnosis is confirmed by duodenal biopsy on gastroscopy.
  • Faecal calprotectin: a neutrophil protein in stool that marks intestinal inflammation. A low result in a young adult without red flags makes IBD unlikely and spares a colonoscopy; a raised result prompts gastroenterology referral. NSAIDs and infection can also raise it.
  • Stool microscopy, culture and PCR: exclude persisting bacterial or parasitic infection, including Giardia.

Other tests that could be considered depending on the picture: gastroscopy and colonoscopy with biopsy when there are red flags or abnormal results, and abdominal imaging if a structural cause is suspected. None is indicated for Jessica now.

Management (eTG Gastrointestinal: irritable bowel syndrome)

  • Explanation and reassurance: a confident, positive diagnosis with a plain explanation of a sensitive gut and gut-brain interaction. IBS is real, common and does not cause cancer or damage the bowel. A good therapeutic relationship improves outcomes.
  • Diet: regular meals, adequate fluids, and less caffeine, alcohol, fatty and gas-producing foods. A time-limited trial of reducing lactose is reasonable given her dairy trigger. If symptoms persist, a dietitian-supervised low FODMAP diet (a short restriction followed by structured reintroduction) helps many patients; long-term unsupervised restriction is avoided.
  • Symptom-directed medicines: antispasmodics (for example mebeverine or hyoscine butylbromide) or peppermint oil for pain and cramping; loperamide when needed for diarrhoea; soluble fibre (psyllium, started low to limit bloating) or an osmotic laxative such as macrogol for constipation. Low-dose tricyclic antidepressants (for example amitriptyline at night) can help persistent pain, and are explained as treating gut nerve sensitivity rather than depression.
  • Psychological and lifestyle: stress, poor sleep and isolation worsen symptoms. Regular exercise, sleep and stress management help; CBT and gut-directed hypnotherapy have evidence in IBS, and a GP mental health treatment plan can give access to Medicare-subsidised psychology.
  • Referral: gastroenterology if red flags develop, if results are abnormal, or if symptoms do not respond to first-line treatment.

Safety netting and follow-up

She should see the GP promptly for rectal bleeding or black stools, weight loss, waking at night with pain or diarrhoea, fevers or persistent vomiting, and go to the ED for severe constant pain, heavy bleeding or feeling faint. Review in about 4 to 6 weeks with a food and symptom diary to judge the lactose trial and treatment and to confirm the diagnosis.
points: In chronic lower GI symptoms, screen every patient for red flags: rectal bleeding, weight loss, nocturnal symptoms, anaemia, fever, a mass, and a family history of colorectal cancer, IBD or coeliac disease. Rectal bleeding with a change in bowel habit warrants colonoscopy even in a young adult.

First-line tests before diagnosing IBS: FBC, CRP, iron studies, B12 and folate, coeliac serology (tTG-IgA with total IgA, on a gluten diet), faecal calprotectin, and stool microscopy, culture and PCR when diarrhoea is prominent.
Coeliac serology is invalid in IgA deficiency and after gluten has been cut out, so always check total IgA and ask about gluten intake.
A faecal calprotectin below 50 µg/g makes IBD unlikely in a young adult without red flags and avoids an unnecessary colonoscopy.

Rome IV: abdominal pain at least weekly with two of: related to defecation, change in frequency, change in form; for 3 months with onset at least 6 months earlier. IBS can follow gastroenteritis (post-infectious IBS).

Make IBS a positive diagnosis and explain it as real, not 'in your head'. Treat with diet (lactose trial, dietitian-led low FODMAP), symptom-directed medicines, stress and psychological therapies, and clear safety netting with review.
